“Samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo sāvakānaṃ evaṃ dhammaṃ deseti – ‘etha tumhe, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānātha, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya viharathā’ti; mayampi kho, āvuso, sāvakānaṃ [V 3.0042] evaṃ dhammaṃ desema – ‘etha tumhe, āvuso, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānātha, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya viharathā’ti. Idha no, āvuso, ko viseso ko adhippayāso kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa amhākaṃ vā, yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya [P 5.0049] vā dhammadesanaṃ anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani”nti?

“‘Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: “Come, bhikkhus, directly know all things; dwell having directly known all things.” We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples thus: “Come, friends, directly know all things; dwell having directly known all things.” Herein, friends, what is the distinction, what is the superiority, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, regarding the teaching of the Dhamma or the instruction?’”

Atha kho te bhikkhū tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ bhāsitaṃ neva abhinandiṃsu nappaṭikkosiṃsu. Anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā [M 3.0296] pakkamiṃsu – “bhagavato [T 5.0052] santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmā”ti.

Then those bhikkhus neither delighted in the statement of those wanderers of other sects nor did they reject it. Not delighting in it and not rejecting it, they rose from their seats and departed, thinking, ‘We shall know the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.’”

Atha kho te bhikkhū sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ –

Then those bhikkhus, having wandered for almsfood in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:

“Idha mayaṃ, bhante, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisimhā. Tesaṃ no, bhante, amhākaṃ etadahosi – ‘atippago kho tāva sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carituṃ; yaṃnūna mayaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyyāmā’ti. Atha kho mayaṃ, bhante, yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkamimhā; upasaṅkamitvā tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ sammodimhā. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdimhā. Ekamantaṃ nisinne kho, bhante, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā amhe etadavocuṃ –

“Venerable sir, today in the morning, having dressed, we took our bowls and robes and entered Sāvatthī for almsfood. To us, venerable sir, this thought occurred: ‘It is still too early to wander in Sāvatthī for almsfood. What if we were to approach the park of the wanderers of other sects?’ Then, venerable sir, we approached the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, we exchanged joyful greetings with those wanderers of other sects. Having concluded the joyful and memorable talk, we sat down to one side. To us who were seated to one side, venerable sir, the wanderers of other sects said this:

‘Samaṇo, āvuso, gotamo sāvakānaṃ evaṃ dhammaṃ deseti – etha tumhe, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānātha, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya viharathāti; mayampi kho, āvuso, sāvakānaṃ evaṃ dhammaṃ desema – etha tumhe, āvuso, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhijānātha, sabbaṃ dhammaṃ abhiññāya viharathāti. Idha no, āvuso, ko viseso ko adhippayāso kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa amhākaṃ vā, yadidaṃ dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesanaṃ anusāsaniyā vā anusāsani’nti?

‘“Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: ‘Come, bhikkhus, directly know all things; dwell having directly known all things.’ We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples thus: ‘Come, friends, directly know all things; dwell having directly known all things.’ Herein, friends, what is the distinction, what is the superiority, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, regarding the teaching of the Dhamma or the instruction?”’

“Atha [V 3.0043] kho [P 5.0050] mayaṃ, bhante, tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ bhāsitaṃ [T 5.0053] neva abhinandimhā nappaṭikkosimhā. Anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamimhā – ‘bhagavato santike etassa bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānissāmā’”ti.

“Then, venerable sir, we neither delighted in the statement of those wanderers of other sects nor did we reject it. Not delighting in it and not rejecting it, we rose from our seats and departed, thinking, ‘We shall know the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.’”

“Evaṃvādino, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘eko, āvuso, pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, dve pañhā dve uddesā dve veyyākaraṇāni, tayo pañhā tayo uddesā tīṇi veyyākaraṇāni, cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇāni, pañca pañhā pañcuddesā pañca veyyākaraṇāni, cha [M 3.0297] pañhā cha uddesā cha veyyākaraṇāni, satta pañhā sattuddesā satta veyyākaraṇāni, aṭṭha pañhā aṭṭhuddesā aṭṭha veyyākaraṇāni, nava pañhā navuddesā nava veyyākaraṇāni, dasa pañhā dasuddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti. Evaṃ puṭṭhā, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā na ceva sampāyissanti, uttari ca vighātaṃ āpajjissanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmiṃ. Nāhaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, passāmi sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya yo imesaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya, aññatra tathāgatena vā tathāgatasāvakena vā ito vā pana sutvā.

‘Bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be spoken to thus: “Friends, there is one question, one brief statement, one explanation; two questions, two brief statements, two explanations; three questions, three brief statements, three explanations; four questions, four brief statements, four explanations; five questions, five brief statements, five explanations; six questions, six brief statements, six explanations; seven questions, seven brief statements, seven explanations; eight questions, eight brief statements, eight explanations; nine questions, nine brief statements, nine explanations; ten questions, ten brief statements, ten explanations.” When asked thus, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects will be unable to answer, and moreover, will fall into vexation. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, it is beyond their domain. I do not see, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind with an explanation of these questions, other than the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from here.’

“‘Eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇa’nti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Ekadhamme, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā [T 5.0054] virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamasmiṃ ekadhamme? ‘Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā’ – imasmiṃ [P 5.0051] kho, bhikkhave, ekadhamme bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇa’nti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘One question, one brief statement, one explanation.’ Indeed, this was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, in regard to one thing, a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In regard to what one thing? ‘All beings are sustained by nutriment.’ It is in regard to this one thing, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘One question, one brief statement, one explanation,’ it was said in reference to this.

“‘Dve pañhā dve uddesā dve veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Dvīsu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu dvīsu? Nāme ca rūpe ca – imesu kho, bhikkhave, dvīsu dhammesu [V 3.0044] bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Dve pañhā dve uddesā dve veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Two questions, two brief statements, two explanations.’ Indeed, this was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, in regard to two things, a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In regard to which two? Name and form. It is in regard to these two things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Two questions, two brief statements, two explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.

“‘Tayo pañhā tayo uddesā tīṇi veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Tīsu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti[M 3.0298]. Katamesu tīsu? Tīsu vedanāsu [T 5.0055] – imesu kho, bhikkhave, tīsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Tayo pañhā tayo uddesā tīṇi veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Three questions, three brief statements, three explanations.’ Indeed, this was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, in regard to three things, a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In regard to which three? The three feelings. It is in regard to these three things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Three questions, three brief statements, three explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.

“‘Cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Catūsu[P 5.0052], bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu catūsu? Catūsu āhāresu – imesu kho, bhikkhave, catūsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Four questions, four brief statements, four explanations.’ Indeed, this was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, in regard to four things, a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In regard to which four? The four kinds of nutriment. It is in regard to these four things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Four questions, four brief statements, four explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.

“‘Pañca pañhā pañcuddesā pañca veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Pañcasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu pañcasu? Pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu – imesu kho, bhikkhave, pañcasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti[T 5.0056]. ‘Pañca pañhā pañcuddesā pañca veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Five questions, five brief statements, five explanations.’ Indeed, this was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, in regard to five things, a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In regard to which five? The five aggregates subject to clinging. It is in regard to these five things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Five questions, five brief statements, five explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.

“‘Cha [V 3.0045] pañhā cha uddesā cha veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Chasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu chasu? Chasu ajjhattikesu āyatanesu – imesu kho, bhikkhave, chasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Cha [P 5.0053] pañhā cha uddesā cha veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Six questions, six brief statements, six explanations’—this, indeed, was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, it is in regard to six things that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which six? In the six internal sense bases. It is in regard to these six things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Six questions, six brief statements, six explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.

“‘Satta [M 3.0299] pañhā sattuddesā satta veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Sattasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu sattasu? Sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu – imesu kho, bhikkhave, sattasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Satta pañhā sattuddesā satta veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Seven questions, seven brief statements, seven explanations’—this, indeed, was said. And in reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, it is in regard to seven things that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which seven? In the seven stations of consciousness. It is in regard to these seven things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Seven questions, seven brief statements, seven explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.”

“‘Aṭṭha pañhā aṭṭhuddesā aṭṭha veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Aṭṭhasu, bhikkhave[T 5.0057], dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu aṭṭhasu? Aṭṭhasu lokadhammesu – imesu kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭhasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno…pe… dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Aṭṭha pañhā aṭṭhuddesā aṭṭha veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Eight questions, eight brief statements, eight explanations’—this, indeed, was said. And in reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, it is in regard to eight things that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which eight? In the eight worldly conditions. It is in regard to these eight things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Eight questions, eight brief statements, eight explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.”

“‘Nava pañhā navuddesā nava veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Navasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu navasu? Navasu sattāvāsesu – imesu [P 5.0054] kho, bhikkhave, navasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī [V 3.0046] sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Nava pañhā navuddesā nava veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

“‘Nine questions, nine brief statements, nine explanations’—this, indeed, was said. And in reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, it is in regard to nine things that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which nine? In the nine abodes of beings. It is in regard to these nine things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Nine questions, nine brief statements, nine explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.”

“‘Dasa pañhā dasuddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Dasasu, bhikkhave, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu dasasu? Dasasu akusalesu kammapathesu [T 5.0058] – imesu kho, bhikkhave, dasasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti[M 3.0300]. ‘Dasa pañhā dasuddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti. Sattamaṃ.

“‘Ten questions, ten brief statements, ten explanations’—this, indeed, was said. And in reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, it is in regard to ten things that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which ten? In the ten unwholesome courses of action. It is in regard to these ten things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu—by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having rightly penetrated the true meaning—makes an end of suffering in this very life. When it was said, ‘Ten questions, ten brief statements, ten explanations,’ it was said in reference to this.” The Seventh.

8. Dutiyamahāpañhāsuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on the Great Questions

28. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kajaṅgalāyaṃ viharati veḷuvane. Atha kho sambahulā kajaṅgalakā upāsakā yena kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā kajaṅgalikaṃ bhikkhuniṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho kajaṅgalakā upāsakā kajaṅgalikaṃ bhikkhuniṃ etadavocuṃ –

28. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Kajaṅgalā, in the Bamboo Grove. Then, many lay followers from Kajaṅgalā approached the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā. Having approached and paid homage to the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the lay followers from Kajaṅgalā said this to the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā:

“Vuttamidaṃ, ayye, bhagavatā mahāpañhesu – ‘eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, dve pañhā dve uddesā dve veyyākaraṇāni, tayo pañhā tayo uddesā tīṇi veyyākaraṇāni, cattāro [P 5.0055] pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇāni, pañca pañhā pañcuddesā pañca veyyākaraṇāni, cha pañhā cha uddesā cha veyyākaraṇāni, satta pañhā sattuddesā satta veyyākaraṇāni, aṭṭha pañhā aṭṭhuddesā aṭṭha veyyākaraṇāni, nava pañhā navuddesā nava veyyākaraṇāni, dasa pañhā dasuddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti. Imassa nu kho, ayye, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa kathaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti?

“Venerable lady, this was said by the Blessed One in the Great Questions: ‘One question, one brief statement, one explanation; two questions, two brief statements, two explanations; three questions, three brief statements, three explanations; four questions, four brief statements, four explanations; five questions, five brief statements, five explanations; six questions, six brief statements, six explanations; seven questions, seven brief statements, seven explanations; eight questions, eight brief statements, eight explanations; nine questions, nine brief statements, nine explanations; ten questions, ten brief statements, ten explanations.’ Venerable lady, how is the meaning of this, which was stated in brief by the Blessed One, to be understood in detail?”

“Na kho panetaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato sammukhā sutaṃ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ, napi manobhāvanīyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sammukhā sutaṃ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ; api ca, yathā mettha khāyati taṃ [V 3.0047] suṇātha, sādhukaṃ [T 5.0059] manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, ayye”ti, kho kajaṅgalakā upāsakā kajaṅgalikāya bhikkhuniyā paccassosuṃ. Kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī etadavoca –

‘Indeed, friends, this was not heard by me in the presence of the Blessed One, nor received in his presence. Nor was it heard or received in the presence of the bhikkhus with developed minds. However, listen to how it appears to me in this matter. Pay careful attention, and I will speak.’ ‘So be it, venerable lady,’ the lay followers from Kajaṅgalā replied to the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā. The bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā said this:

“‘Eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇa’nti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Ekadhamme, āvuso, bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamasmiṃ ekadhamme? Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā – imasmiṃ kho, āvuso, ekadhamme bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme [M 3.0301] dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇanti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘“One question, one summary, one explanation”—indeed, this was said by the Blessed One. In reference to what was this said? Friends, in regard to one principle, a bhikkhu, by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In which one principle? “All beings subsist on nutriment.” Indeed, friends, it is in regard to this one principle that a bhikkhu, by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. That which was stated by the Blessed One as, “One question, one summary, one explanation,” was stated in reference to this.

“‘Dve [P 5.0056] pañhā dve uddesā dve veyyākaraṇānī’ti iti, kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Dvīsu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu dvīsu? Nāme ca rūpe ca…pe… [T 5.0060] katamesu tīsu? Tīsu vedanāsu – imesu kho, āvuso, tīsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Tayo pañhā tayo uddesā tīṇi veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘“Two questions, two summaries, and two explanations”—indeed, this was said by the Blessed One. In reference to what was this said? Friends, in regard to two principles, a bhikkhu, by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In which two? In name and form... In which three? In the three feelings. Indeed, friends, it is in regard to these three principles that a bhikkhu, by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. That which was stated by the Blessed One as, “Three questions, three summaries, and three explanations,” was stated in reference to this.

“‘Cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Catūsu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu catūsu? Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu – imesu kho, āvuso, catūsu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Cattāro pañhā cattāro uddesā cattāri veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘“Four questions, four summaries, and four explanations”—indeed, this was said by the Blessed One. In reference to what was this said? Friends, in regard to four principles, a bhikkhu with a mind rightly developed, by rightly seeing the limit and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In which four? In the four foundations of mindfulness. Indeed, friends, it is in regard to these four principles that a bhikkhu with a mind rightly developed, by rightly seeing the limit and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. That which was stated by the Blessed One as, “Four questions, four summaries, and four explanations,” was stated in reference to this.

“‘Pañca [V 3.0048] pañhā pañcuddesā pañca veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Pañcasu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu pañcasu? Pañcasu indriyesu…pe… katamesu chasu? Chasu [T 5.0061][P 5.0057] nissaraṇīyāsu dhātūsu…pe… katamesu sattasu? Sattasu bojjhaṅgesu…pe… katamesu aṭṭhasu? Aṭṭhasu ariyaaṭṭhaṅgikamaggesu – imesu kho, āvuso, aṭṭhasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Aṭṭha pañhā aṭṭhuddesā aṭṭha veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘“Five questions, five summaries, and five explanations”—indeed, this was said by the Blessed One. In reference to what was this said? Friends, in regard to five principles, a bhikkhu with a mind rightly developed, by rightly seeing the limit and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In which five? In the five faculties... In which six? In the six elements of escape... In which seven? In the seven factors of enlightenment... In which eight? In the Noble Eightfold Path. Indeed, friends, it is in regard to these eight principles that a bhikkhu with a mind rightly developed, by rightly seeing the limit and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. That which was stated by the Blessed One as, “Eight questions, eight summaries, and eight explanations,” was stated in reference to this.

“‘Nava [M 3.0302] pañhā navuddesā nava veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Navasu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu navasu? Navasu sattāvāsesu – imesu kho, āvuso, navasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā nibbindamāno sammā virajjamāno sammā vimuccamāno sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Nava pañhā navuddesā nava veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘“Nine questions, nine summaries, and nine explanations”—indeed, this was said by the Blessed One. In reference to what was this said? Friends, in regard to nine principles, a bhikkhu, by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In which nine? In the nine abodes of beings. Indeed, friends, it is in regard to these nine principles that a bhikkhu, by rightly becoming disenchanted, rightly becoming dispassionate, rightly being liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. That which was stated by the Blessed One as, “Nine questions, nine summaries, and nine explanations,” was stated in reference to this.’

“‘Dasa pañhā dasuddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Dasasu, āvuso, dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. Katamesu dasasu? Dasasu kusalesu kammapathesu – imesu [P 5.0058] kho, āvuso, dasasu dhammesu bhikkhu sammā subhāvitacitto sammā pariyantadassāvī sammadatthaṃ abhisamecca diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hoti. ‘Dasa pañhā dasuddesā [T 5.0062] dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti, iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā idametaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ.

‘“Ten questions, ten summaries, and ten explanations”—indeed, this was said by the Blessed One. In reference to what was this said? Friends, in regard to ten principles, a bhikkhu with a mind rightly developed, by rightly seeing the limit and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. In which ten? In the ten wholesome courses of action. Indeed, friends, it is in regard to these ten principles that a bhikkhu with a mind rightly developed, by rightly seeing the limit and having thoroughly understood the true meaning, becomes an ender of suffering in this very life. That which was stated by the Blessed One as, “Ten questions, ten summaries, and ten explanations,” was stated in reference to this.’

“Iti kho, āvuso, yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitāsu mahāpañhāsu – ‘eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ…pe… dasa pañhā dasuddesā dasa veyyākaraṇānī’ti, imassa kho ahaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ [V 3.0049] ājānāmi. Ākaṅkhamānā ca pana tumhe, āvuso, bhagavantaññeva upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha. Yathā vo yathā kho (ka.), yathā no (bahūsu) a. ni. 10.115, 172 pana pāṭhabhedo natthi bhagavā byākaroti tathā naṃ dhāreyyāthā”ti. “Evaṃ, ayye”ti kho kajaṅgalakā upāsakā kajaṅgalikāya kho bhikkhuniyā bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā kajaṅgalikaṃ bhikkhuniṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho kajaṅgalakā upāsakā yāvatako ahosi kajaṅgalikāya bhikkhuniyā saddhiṃ kathāsallāpo, taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ.

‘Thus, friends, of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One in the Great Questions—“one question, one summary, and one exposition… ten questions, ten summaries, and ten expositions”—I understand the meaning in detail thus. But if you wish, friends, you should approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should remember it.’ ‘Very well, venerable lady,’ replied the lay followers of Kajaṅgala. Delighted and approving of what the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā had said, they rose from their seats, paid homage to the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā, circumambulated her with their right side, and then went to the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the lay followers of Kajaṅgala reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation they had had with the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā.

“Sādhu [M 3.0303] sādhu, gahapatayo! Paṇḍitā, gahapatayo, kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī. Mahāpaññā, gahapatayo, kajaṅgalikā bhikkhunī. Mañcepi tumhe, gahapatayo, upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ paṭipuccheyyātha, ahampi cetaṃ evamevaṃ [P 5.0059] evameva (ka.) ma. ni. 1.205 passitabbaṃ byākareyyaṃ yathā taṃ kajaṅgalikāya bhikkhuniyā byākataṃ. Eso ceva tassa eso cevetassa (ma. ni. 1.205) attho. Evañca naṃ dhāreyyāthā”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Good, good, householders! The bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā is wise, householders. The bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā is of great wisdom, householders. Even if you, householders, were to approach me and ask about this matter, I too would explain it in exactly the same way as it has been explained by the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā. That is indeed its meaning. And thus you should remember it.” Eighth.

9. Paṭhamakosalasuttaṃ

9. The First Discourse on Kosala

29. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, kāsikosalā, yāvatā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa vijitaṃ vijite (sī. ka.), rājā tattha pasenadi kosalo aggamakkhāyati. Raññopi [T 5.0063] kho, bhikkhave, pasenadissa kosalassa attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

29. “Bhikkhus, as far as the Kasi and Kosala countries extend, as far as the domain of King Pasenadi of Kosala reaches, King Pasenadi of Kosala is declared the foremost there. Yet even for King Pasenadi of Kosala, bhikkhus, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost; what need is there to speak of the inferior?

“Yāvatā, bhikkhave, candimasūriyā pariharanti disā bhanti virocamānā, tāva sahassadhā loko. Tasmiṃ sahassadhā loke sahassaṃ candānaṃ sahassaṃ sūriyānaṃ suriyānaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) sahassaṃ sinerupabbatarājānaṃ sahassaṃ jambudīpānaṃ sahassaṃ aparagoyānānaṃ sahassaṃ uttarakurūnaṃ sahassaṃ pubbavidehānaṃ cattāri mahāsamuddasahassāni cattāri mahārājasahassāni sahassaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ sahassaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahassaṃ yāmānaṃ sahassaṃ tusitānaṃ sahassaṃ nimmānaratīnaṃ sahassaṃ paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ sahassaṃ brahmalokānaṃ. Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sahassī lokadhātu, mahābrahmā tattha [P 5.0060] aggamakkhāyati. Mahābrahmunopi kho, bhikkhave, attheva aññathattaṃ atthi [V 3.0050] vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Bhikkhus, as far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and being resplendent over the quarters, so far extends the thousandfold world-sphere. In that thousandfold world-sphere, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sinerus, kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand realms of the Four Great Kings, a thousand realms of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, a thousand realms of the Yāma devas, a thousand realms of the Tusita devas, a thousand realms of the Nimmānaratī devas, a thousand realms of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, and a thousand Brahmā worlds. Bhikkhus, as far as this thousandfold world-sphere extends, Mahābrahmā is declared the foremost there. Yet even for Mahābrahmā, bhikkhus, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost; what need is there to speak of the inferior?

“Hoti so, bhikkhave, samayo yaṃ ayaṃ loko saṃvaṭṭati. Saṃvaṭṭamāne, bhikkhave, loke yebhuyyena sattā ābhassarasaṃvattanikā ābhassaravattanikā (sī. syā.) bhavanti. Te tattha honti manomayā pītibhakkhā sayaṃpabhā antalikkhecarā subhaṭṭhāyino ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Saṃvaṭṭamāne, bhikkhave, loke ābhassarā [M 3.0304] devā aggamakkhāyanti. Ābhassarānampi kho, bhikkhave, devānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati[T 5.0064]. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Bhikkhus, there is a time when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhassara Brahmā realm. There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, traveling through the sky, abiding in splendor, and they remain for a very long time. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, the Ābhassara devas are declared the foremost. Yet even for the Ābhassara devas, bhikkhus, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost; what need is there to speak of the inferior?

a. ni. 10.25 “Dasayimāni, bhikkhave, kasiṇāyatanāni. Katamāni dasa? Pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ; āpokasiṇameko sañjānāti…pe… tejokasiṇameko sañjānāti… vāyokasiṇameko sañjānāti… nīlakasiṇameko sañjānāti… pītakasiṇameko sañjānāti… lohitakasiṇameko sañjānāti… odātakasiṇameko sañjānāti… ākāsakasiṇameko sañjānāti… viññāṇakasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, dasa kasiṇāyatanāni.

“Bhikkhus, there are these ten kasiṇa bases. What ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa: above, below, and across, as non-dual and immeasurable. One perceives the water kasiṇa… one perceives the fire kasiṇa… one perceives the air kasiṇa… one perceives the blue kasiṇa… one perceives the yellow kasiṇa… one perceives the red kasiṇa… one perceives the white kasiṇa… one perceives the space kasiṇa… one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa: above, below, and across, as non-dual and immeasurable. These, bhikkhus, are the ten kasiṇa bases.”

“Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, imesaṃ dasannaṃ kasiṇāyatanānaṃ yadidaṃ viññāṇakasiṇaṃ eko sañjānāti uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Evaṃsaññinopi kho, bhikkhave, santi sattā. Evaṃsaññīnampi kho, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ[P 5.0061], bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among these ten kasiṇa bases: that one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, and across, as non-dual and immeasurable. Bhikkhus, there are indeed beings with such a perception. Yet even for beings with such a perception, bhikkhus, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost; what need is there to speak of the inferior?”

dī. ni. 3.338, 358; a. ni. 8.64 “Aṭṭhimāni, bhikkhave, abhibhāyatanāni. Katamāni aṭṭha? Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, there are these eight bases of mastery. What eight? One who is percipient of form internally sees external forms, limited, of beautiful and ugly appearance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the first basis of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ [V 3.0051] rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“One who is percipient of form internally sees external forms, immeasurable, of beautiful and ugly appearance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the second basis of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni; ‘tāni [T 5.0065] abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“One who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms, limited, of beautiful and ugly appearance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the third sphere of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ [M 3.0305] arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ catutthaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“One who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms, immeasurable, of beautiful and ugly appearance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fourth sphere of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma umāpupphaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ; evamevaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“One who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, and of blue radiance. Just as a flax flower is blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, and of blue radiance, or just as a cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, and of blue radiance; even so, one who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, and of blue radiance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fifth sphere of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma kaṇikārapupphaṃ pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ [P 5.0062] ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ; evamevaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“One who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, and of yellow radiance. Just as a kaṇikāra flower is yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, and of yellow radiance, or just as a cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, and of yellow radiance; even so, one who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, and of yellow radiance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the sixth sphere of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma bandhujīvakapupphaṃ [T 5.0066] lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ; evamevaṃ ajjhattaṃ [V 3.0052] arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ sattamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

“One who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are red, of red color, of red appearance, and of red radiance. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, of red appearance, and of red radiance, or just as a cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is red, of red color, of red appearance, and of red radiance; even so, one who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are red, of red color, of red appearance, and of red radiance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the seventh sphere of mastery.”

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma osadhitārakā odātā odātavaṇṇā odātanidassanā odātanibhāsā, seyyathā [M 3.0306] vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ odātaṃ odātavaṇṇaṃ odātanidassanaṃ odātanibhāsaṃ; evamevaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni.

“One who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are white, of white color, of white appearance, and of white radiance. Just as the morning star is white, of white color, of white appearance, and of white radiance, or just as a cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is white, of white color, of white appearance, and of white radiance; even so, one who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are white, of white color, of white appearance, and of white radiance. Having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the eighth sphere of mastery. Monks, these are indeed the eight spheres of mastery.”

“Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ abhibhāyatanānaṃ yadidaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni; ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti, evaṃsaññī hoti. Evaṃsaññinopi kho, bhikkhave, santi sattā. Evaṃsaññīnampi kho, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ [P 5.0063] atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ [T 5.0067] passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Monks, this is the foremost among these eight spheres of mastery, namely: that one who is not percipient of form internally sees external forms that are white, of white color, of white appearance, and of white radiance; having overcome them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ Monks, there are indeed beings who are percipient in this way. Yet for such percipient beings, monks, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest; what then to say of the inferior?”

“Catasso imā, bhikkhave, paṭipadā. Katamā catasso? Dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā, dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā, sukhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā, sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā – imā kho, bhikkhave, catasso paṭipadā.

“Monks, there are these four courses of practice. What four? Painful practice with slow direct knowledge, painful practice with quick direct knowledge, pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Monks, these are indeed the four courses of practice.”

“Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, imāsaṃ catunnaṃ paṭipadānaṃ yadidaṃ sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā. Evaṃpaṭipannāpi kho, bhikkhave, santi sattā. Evaṃpaṭipannānampi kho, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Monks, this is the foremost among these four courses of practice, namely, the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Monks, there are indeed beings who have undertaken such a practice. Yet for such beings who have undertaken this practice, monks, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest; what then to say of the inferior?”

“Catasso [V 3.0053] imā, bhikkhave, saññā. Katamā catasso? Parittameko sañjānāti, mahaggatameko sañjānāti, appamāṇameko sañjānāti, ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanameko sañjānāti – imā kho, bhikkhave, catasso saññā.

“Monks, there are these four perceptions. What four? A certain person perceives the limited; a certain person perceives the exalted; a certain person perceives the immeasurable; and a certain person perceives the base of nothingness as ‘There is nothing.’ Monks, these are indeed the four perceptions.”

“Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, imāsaṃ catunnaṃ saññānaṃ yadidaṃ ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanameko sañjānāti. Evaṃsaññinopi kho, bhikkhave, santi sattā. Evaṃsaññīnampi kho, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Monks, this is the foremost among these four perceptions, namely, that a certain person perceives the base of nothingness as ‘There is nothing.’ Monks, there are indeed beings who are percipient in this way. Yet for such percipient beings, monks, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest; what then to say of the inferior?”

“Etadaggaṃ[M 3.0307], bhikkhave, bāhirakānaṃ diṭṭhigatānaṃ yadidaṃ ‘no cassaṃ, no ca me siyā, na bhavissāmi, na me bhavissatī’ti. Evaṃdiṭṭhino, bhikkhave[T 5.0068], etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – ‘yā cāyaṃ bhave appaṭikulyatā, sā cassa na [P 5.0064] bhavissati; yā cāyaṃ bhavanirodhe pāṭikulyatā, sā cassa na bhavissatī’ti. Evaṃdiṭṭhinopi kho, bhikkhave, santi sattā. Evaṃdiṭṭhīnampi kho, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

Monks, this is the foremost among the views of outsiders, namely, this view: ‘If I had not existed, nothing would be mine; I will not exist, and nothing will be mine.’ For one with such a view, monks, this is to be expected: that he will not find existence agreeable, and he will not find the cessation of existence disagreeable. Monks, there are indeed beings with such a view. Yet for such beings with this view, monks, there is indeed alteration, there is change. Seeing this, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that view. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest; what then to say of the inferior?

“Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā paramatthavisuddhiṃ paññāpenti. Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, paramatthavisuddhiṃ paññāpentānaṃ yadidaṃ sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Te tadabhiññāya tassa sacchikiriyāya dhammaṃ desenti. Evaṃvādinopi kho, bhikkhave, santi sattā. Evaṃvādīnampi kho, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ attheva aññathattaṃ atthi vipariṇāmo. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako tasmimpi nibbindati. Tasmiṃ nibbindanto agge virajjati, pageva hīnasmiṃ.

“Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim ultimate purity. This, monks, is the foremost among those who proclaim ultimate purity: namely, that by completely transcending the base of nothingness, one attains and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having known it through direct knowledge, they teach the Dhamma for its realization. Monks, there are indeed beings who hold such a doctrine. Yet for those beings who hold such a doctrine, monks, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing this, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with it, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest; what then to say of the inferior?”

“Santi, bhikkhave, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññāpenti. Etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ paññāpentānaṃ yadidaṃ channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādā vimokkho. Evaṃvādiṃ kho maṃ, bhikkhave, evamakkhāyiṃ eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā asatā tucchā musā abhūtena abbhācikkhanti – ‘samaṇo [V 3.0054] gotamo na kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti, na [T 5.0069] rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti, na vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpetī’ti. Kāmānañcāhaṃ[P 5.0065], bhikkhave, pariññaṃ paññāpemi, rūpānañca pariññaṃ paññāpemi, vedanānañca pariññaṃ paññāpemi, diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītibhūto anupādā parinibbānaṃ paññāpemī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim the ultimate Nibbāna in this very life. This, monks, is the foremost among those who proclaim the ultimate Nibbāna in this very life: namely, the liberation through non-clinging, having understood as they truly are the origin, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to the six bases for contact. Monks, when I speak and declare thus, some ascetics and brahmins misrepresent me with what is untrue, void, false, and baseless, saying: ‘The ascetic Gotama does not proclaim the full understanding of sensual pleasures, he does not proclaim the full understanding of forms, he does not proclaim the full understanding of feelings.’ But, monks, I do proclaim the full understanding of sensual pleasures, I do proclaim the full understanding of forms, and I do proclaim the full understanding of feelings. In this very life, being without craving, extinguished, and cooled, I proclaim the final Nibbāna through non-clinging.” The ninth.

10. Dutiyakosalasuttaṃ

10. The Second Kosala Sutta

30. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tena kho pana samayena rājā pasenadi kosalo uyyodhikā nivatto hoti vijitasaṅgāmo laddhādhippāyo. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena ārāmo tena pāyāsi. Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi, yānena gantvā yānā paccorohitvā pattikova ārāmaṃ pāvisi. Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū [M 3.0308] abbhokāse caṅkamanti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā te bhikkhū etadavoca – “kahaṃ nu kho, bhante, bhagavā etarahi viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Dassanakāmā hi mayaṃ, bhante, taṃ bhagavantaṃ arahantaṃ sammāsambuddha”nti. “Eso, mahārāja, vihāro saṃvutadvāro. Tena appasaddo upasaṅkamitvā ataramāno ālindaṃ pavisitvā ukkāsitvā aggaḷaṃ ākoṭehi; vivarissati te bhagavā dvāra”nti.

30. On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, at Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, having conquered in battle and achieved his aim, had returned from a military expedition. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the monastery. He went by vehicle as far as the ground was passable for a vehicle, then dismounted from his vehicle and entered the monastery on foot. Now at that time, a number of monks were walking in the open air. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached those monks and, having approached them, said this: “Venerable sirs, where is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwelling at present? For we desire to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.” “That, great king, is the dwelling with the closed door. Approach it making little sound and, without hurrying, enter the porch, clear your throat, and knock on the door-bar. The Blessed One will open the door for you.”

Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena so vihāro saṃvutadvāro, tena appasaddo upasaṅkamitvā ataramāno ālindaṃ pavisitvā ukkāsitvā aggaḷaṃ ākoṭesi. Vivari bhagavā dvāraṃ. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo vihāraṃ pavisitvā bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavato pādāni mukhena [T 5.0070] ca paricumbati pāṇīhi ca parisambāhati nāmañca sāveti – “rājāhaṃ, bhante, pasenadi kosalo; rājāhaṃ, bhante[P 5.0066], pasenadi kosalo”ti.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached that dwelling with the closed door, making little sound and, without hurrying, entered the porch, cleared his throat, and knocked on the door-bar. The Blessed One opened the door. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having entered the dwelling, fell with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, and massaged them with his hands, and announced his name: “Venerable sir, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala; venerable sir, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala.”

“Kaṃ pana tvaṃ, mahārāja, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno imasmiṃ sarīre evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karosi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsesī”ti? “Kataññutaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, kataveditaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

“Seeing what special reason, great king, do you perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to this body?” “Venerable sir, it is because I see my gratitude and thankfulness that I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Bhagavā [V 3.0055] hi, bhante, bahujanahitāya paṭipanno bahujanasukhāya bahuno janassa ariye ñāye patiṭṭhāpitā yadidaṃ kalyāṇadhammatāya kusaladhammatāya. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā bahujanahitāya paṭipanno bahujanasukhāya bahuno janassa ariye ñāye patiṭṭhāpitā yadidaṃ kalyāṇadhammatāya kusaladhammatāya, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

“For, venerable sir, the Blessed One is one who practices for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people; he has established many people in the noble method, that is, in what is of a virtuous nature and what is of a wholesome nature. Venerable sir, it is because the Blessed One is one who practices for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, and has established many people in the noble method, that is, in what is of a virtuous nature and what is of a wholesome nature—seeing this special reason, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā sīlavā vuddhasīlo ariyasīlo kusalasīlo kusalasīlena samannāgato. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā sīlavā vuddhasīlo ariyasīlo kusalasīlo kusalasīlena samannāgato, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

“And furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is virtuous, possesses developed virtue, possesses noble virtue, possesses wholesome virtue, and is endowed with wholesome virtue. Venerable sir, it is because the Blessed One is virtuous, possesses developed virtue, possesses noble virtue, possesses wholesome virtue, and is endowed with wholesome virtue—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna [M 3.0309] caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā dīgharattaṃ āraññiko, araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevati. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā dīgharattaṃ āraññiko, araññavanapatthāni [P 5.0067] pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevati, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One has for a long time been a forest-dweller; he resorts to remote lodgings in forest groves. Venerable sir, it is because the Blessed One has for a long time been a forest-dweller and resorts to remote lodgings in forest groves—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho [T 5.0071] itarītaracīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā santuṭṭho itarītaracīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi. “Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive. Since the Blessed One is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One. Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Since the Blessed One is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā yāyaṃ kathā abhisallekhikā cetovivaraṇasappāyā, seyyathidaṃ – appicchakathā santuṭṭhikathā pavivekakathā asaṃsaggakathā vīriyārambhakathā sīlakathā samādhikathā [V 3.0056] paññākathā vimuttikathā vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā, evarūpāya kathāya nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā yāyaṃ kathā abhisallekhikā cetovivaraṇasappāyā, seyyathidaṃ – appicchakathā…pe… vimuttiñāṇadassanakathā, evarūpāya kathāya nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, such talk as is concerned with effacement, conducive to the opening up of the heart; that is, talk on fewness of wishes, on contentment, on seclusion, on non-association, on arousing energy, on virtue, on concentration, on wisdom, on liberation, and on the knowledge and vision of liberation. Since the Blessed One obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, such talk as is concerned with effacement, conducive to the opening up of the heart—that is, talk on fewness of wishes… on the knowledge and vision of liberation—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ nikāmalābhī [P 5.0068] akicchalābhī akasiralābhī. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ [T 5.0072] nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant abidings in this very life. Since the Blessed One obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant abidings in this very life—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna [M 3.0310] caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so-named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There, too, I was so-named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-span. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Since the Blessed One recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births… thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā [T 5.0073] vacīduccaritena samannāgatā [V 3.0057] manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā [P 5.0069] micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā; ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti, iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāti, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations—and he understands beings as faring on according to their kamma: ‘These good beings, endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, revilers of the noble ones, holders of wrong view who have undertaken kamma based on wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, in hell. But those other good beings, endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, holders of right view who have undertaken kamma based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn… and understands beings as faring on according to their kamma. Since the Blessed One with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human… understands beings as faring on according to their kamma—seeing this special reason as well, venerable sir, I perform such an act of supreme humility and show such an offering of loving-kindness to the Blessed One.

“Puna [M 3.0311] caparaṃ, bhante, bhagavā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Yampi, bhante, bhagavā āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ…pe… sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati, idampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasaṃ sampassamāno bhagavati evarūpaṃ paramanipaccakāraṃ karomi, mettūpahāraṃ upadaṃsemi.

Furthermore, venerable sir, through the destruction of the taints, the Blessed One, in this very life, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. Since the Blessed One, venerable sir, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge—seeing this very reason, venerable sir, I pay such supreme homage to the Blessed One and present this offering of loving-kindness.

“Handa ca dāni mayaṃ, bhante, gacchāma. Bahukiccā mayaṃ bahukaraṇīyā”ti. “Yassa dāni tvaṃ, mahārāja, kālaṃ maññasī”ti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ [T 5.0074] katvā pakkāmīti. Dasamaṃ.

“Well now, venerable sir, we must go. We are busy and have much to do.” “Now, great king, it is for you to do as you see fit.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, circumambulating him to the right, departed. The tenth.

Mahāvaggo tatiyo.

The Third Great Chapter.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Sīhādhivutti [P 5.0070] kāyena, cundena kasiṇena ca;

Kāḷī ca dve mahāpañhā, kosalehi pare duveti.

The Lion, Conviction, With the Body, With Cunda, and With the Kasiṇa; Kāḷī, the Two Great Questions, and two others concerning the Kosalans.

4. Upālivaggo

4. 4. The Chapter on Upāli

1. Upālisuttaṃ

1. 1. The Discourse concerning Upāli

31. Atha [V 3.0058] kho āyasmā upāli yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā upāli bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kati nu kho, bhante, atthavase paṭicca tathāgatena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ uddiṭṭha”nti?

31. Then the Venerable Upāli went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated thus, the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, for the sake of how many benefits has the training rule been laid down for the disciples by the Tathāgata, and the Pātimokkha set forth?”

“Dasa kho, upāli, atthavase paṭicca tathāgatena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ. Katame dasa? Saṅghasuṭṭhutāya, saṅghaphāsutāya, dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāya, pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāya, diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya, appasannānaṃ pasādāya, pasannānaṃ bhiyyobhāvāya, saddhammaṭṭhitiyā, vinayānuggahāya – ime kho, upāli, dasa atthavase paṭicca tathāgatena sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, pātimokkhaṃ uddiṭṭha”nti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Upāli, it is for the sake of ten benefits that the training rule has been laid down for the disciples by the Tathāgata, and the Pātimokkha set forth. What are the ten? For the excellence of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of corrupt individuals, for the comfortable living of virtuous bhikkhus, for the guarding against taints in the present life, for the warding off of taints in a future life, for inspiring confidence in those not yet confident, for the increase of confidence in those who are confident, for the stability of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the discipline. It is for the sake of these ten benefits, Upāli, that the training rule has been laid down for the disciples by the Tathāgata, and the Pātimokkha set forth.” The first.

2. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanāsuttaṃ

2. 2. The Discourse on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha

32. “Kati [M 3.0312] nu kho, bhante, pātimokkhaṭṭhapanā”ti? “Dasa kho, upāli, pātimokkhaṭṭhapanā. Katame dasa? Pārājiko tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno hoti[T 5.0075], pārājikakathā vippakatā hoti, anupasampanno tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno [P 5.0071] hoti, anupasampannakathā vippakatā hoti, sikkhaṃ paccakkhātako tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno hoti, sikkhaṃ paccakkhātakakathā vippakatā hoti, paṇḍako tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno hoti, paṇḍakakathā vippakatā hoti, bhikkhunidūsako tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno hoti, bhikkhunidūsakakathā vippakatā hoti – ime kho, upāli, dasa pātimokkhaṭṭhapanā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

32. “Venerable sir, how many grounds are there for suspending the Pātimokkha?” “There are ten grounds for suspending the Pātimokkha, Upāli. What are the ten? A person who has committed a pārājika offense is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning a pārājika offense is unfinished; an unordained person is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning an unordained person is unfinished; one who has renounced the training is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning one who has renounced the training is unfinished; a paṇḍaka is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning a paṇḍaka is unfinished; a corrupter of a bhikkhunī is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning a corrupter of a bhikkhunī is unfinished. These, Upāli, are the ten grounds for suspending the Pātimokkha.” The second.

3. Ubbāhikāsuttaṃ

3. 3. The Discourse on Appointment

33. cūḷava. 231 “Katihi [V 3.0059] nu kho, bhante, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu ubbāhikāya sammannitabbo”ti? “Dasahi kho, upāli, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu ubbāhikāya sammannitabbo. Katamehi dasahi? Idhupāli, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti; pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu; bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo, ye te dhammā ādikalyāṇā majjhekalyāṇā pariyosānakalyāṇā sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ satthā sabyañjanā (sī.) evamuparipi kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ abhivadanti, tathārūpāssa dhammā bahussutā honti dhātā vacasā paricitā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā; ubhayāni kho panassa pātimokkhāni vitthārena svāgatāni honti suvibhattāni suppavattīni suvinicchitāni suttaso anubyañjanaso; vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti asaṃhīro; paṭibalo hoti ubho atthapaccatthike saññāpetuṃ paññāpetuṃ nijjhāpetuṃ pekkhetuṃ pasādetuṃ; adhikaraṇasamuppādavūpasamakusalo [P 5.0072] hoti – adhikaraṇaṃ jānāti; adhikaraṇasamudayaṃ jānāti; adhikaraṇanirodhaṃ [T 5.0076] jānāti; adhikaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ jānāti. Imehi kho, upāli, dasahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu ubbāhikāya sammannitabbo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

33. “Venerable sir, endowed with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be appointed by a formal act of the Saṅgha?” “Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with ten qualities should be appointed by a formal act of the Saṅgha. With which ten? Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, is accomplished in conduct and resort, and sees danger in the slightest faults; he undertakes and trains in the training rules. He is learned, remembers what he has heard, and has accumulated learning. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the spiritual life that is entirely complete and pure—such teachings have been heard by him in abundance, are borne in mind, recited verbally, examined mentally, and well penetrated by view. Furthermore, both Pātimokkhas are well transmitted to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-determined, both according to the rules and according to the details. He is established in the Vinaya and is unwavering. He is capable of making both opposing parties understand, of explaining to them, making them reflect, consider, and find confidence. He is skilled in the arising and settling of legal issues: he knows a legal issue, he knows the origin of a legal issue, he knows the cessation of a legal issue, and he knows the way leading to the cessation of a legal issue. Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities should be appointed by a formal act of the Saṅgha.” The third.

4. Upasampadāsuttaṃ

4. 4. The Discourse on Ordination

34. “Katihi [M 3.0313] nu kho, bhante, dhammehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā upasampādetabba”nti? “Dasahi kho, upāli, dhammehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā upasampādetabbaṃ. Katamehi dasahi? Idhupāli, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu; bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo, ye te dhammā ādikalyāṇā majjhekalyāṇā pariyosānakalyāṇā sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ abhivadanti, tathārūpāssa dhammā bahussutā honti dhātā vacasā paricitā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā; pātimokkhaṃ kho panassa vitthārena svāgataṃ hoti suvibhattaṃ suppavattaṃ suvinicchitaṃ suttaso anubyañjanaso; paṭibalo hoti gilānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ vā upaṭṭhāpetuṃ vā; paṭibalo hoti anabhiratiṃ vūpakāsetuṃ vā [V 3.0060] vūpakāsāpetuṃ vā; paṭibalo hoti uppannaṃ kukkuccaṃ dhammato vinodetuṃ; paṭibalo hoti uppannaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ dhammato vivecetuṃ; paṭibalo hoti adhisīle samādapetuṃ; paṭibalo hoti adhicitte samādapetuṃ; paṭibalo hoti adhipaññāya samādapetuṃ. Imehi kho, upāli, dasahi dhammehi samannāgatena bhikkhunā upasampādetabba”nti. Catutthaṃ.

34. “Venerable sir, endowed with how many qualities may a bhikkhu give ordination?” “Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with ten qualities may give ordination. With which ten? Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, is accomplished in conduct and resort, and sees danger in the slightest faults; he undertakes and trains in the training rules. He is of great learning, remembers what he has heard, and has accumulated what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the holy life that is entirely complete and pure—such teachings have been much heard by him, are borne in mind, familiarized by recitation, mentally examined, and well penetrated by view.
